c.tagline: Korea's soul-food capital, where 800 hanok houses cradle the birthplace of bibimbap.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered and cheap; most residents summon them through the Kakao T app, which shows the fare and lets you pay by registered card. Street hails are also easy in the center.

emergency.note: Dial 112 for police and 119 for fire or ambulance; the 1330 Korea Travel Hotline offers 24/7 English assistance.

hood_desc: The famous cluster of more than 800 traditional tile-roofed hanok houses, home to Gyeonggijeon Shrine, Jeondong Catholic Cathedral, hanji paper workshops, and endless street food; the sightseeing core where most visitors base themselves.
The modern downtown north of the hanok quarter around the historic Gaeksa guesthouse pavilion, thick with shops, cafes, cosmetics stores, and youthful nightlife; best for shopping and going out.
A calmer district north of the center built around Deokjin Park and its lotus-covered pond and university campuses; leafy, local, and relaxed, with cheaper stays.

water.note: Tap water is safe, though locals commonly drink bottled or filtered.

transit.pay: Buy or top up a T-money or Hanaro transit card at any convenience store (GS25, CU, 7-Eleven) and tap it on city buses for a base fare of about 1,500 won (~US$1.10); cash is accepted but exact change is expected. The same card works nationwide and on taxis.
transit.hours: City buses run roughly 5:30am to 11pm; there is no subway, so late-night trips rely on taxis, which are plentiful and inexpensive.
transit.note: Jeonju has no metro — the compact hanok village is best explored on foot, while frequent city buses connect the downtown, Deokjin Park, and Jeonju Station a few kilometres northeast of the center.

train: Jeonju Station (KTX / SRT via Iksan, Jeolla Line)

transit.m: Intercity bus Gunsan–Jeonju + city bus (~90 min)
KTX to Jeonju via Yongsan/Seoul from Gimpo (GMP) area (~2 hr)
Airport limousine bus from Muan Int'l (MWX) via Gwangju

tip.r: Tipping is not customary or expected in South Korea; there is no need to tip taxis, restaurants, or hotels.

food.name: Jeonju Bibimbap
food.desc: The definitive version: rice cooked in beef broth, some thirty toppings, yellow mung-bean jelly and raw beef, mixed in a brass bowl with Sunchang gochujang.

places.name: Hankookjib
places.note: Serving bibimbap for over 70 years and among the first Korean restaurants in the Michelin Guide.

places.name: Gogung Suragan
places.note: Hanok Village branch of the celebrated Gogung, staff in hanbok and a full banchan spread.

places.name: Gajok Hoegwan
places.note: Old-school local favourite known for the beef-broth rice and dolsot version.

food.name: Kongnamul Gukbap
food.desc: Jeonju's hangover cure: rice in a clear bean-sprout broth with squid, egg and chilli, bubbling in a stone pot with a side of salted shrimp.

places.name: Waengi Kongnamul Gukbap
places.note: Open around the clock and packed at dawn with market traders and late-night drinkers.

places.name: Sambaekjip
places.note: Historic bean-sprout soup house, one of the names credited with making the dish famous.

places.name: Hyundaeok
places.note: Jeonju-born chain doing a lighter, cleaner broth with the egg stirred in separately.

food.name: Jeonju Hanjeongsik
food.desc: The Jeolla banquet: twenty or more small dishes of pickles, jeon, braises, grilled fish and greens crowding the table around rice and soup.

places.name: Gogung Suragan
places.note: Royal-style course menus in a traditional hanok setting, easy for visitors to order.

places.name: Hanok Village hanjeongsik houses
places.note: Several courtyard restaurants along the village lanes serve set banquets for two or more.

places.name: Gajok Hoegwan
places.note: Local institution whose set menus come with a long parade of Jeolla side dishes.

food.name: Pi-Sundae and Sundae-Guk
food.desc: Jeonju-style blood sausage, dense with glutinous rice and vegetables, eaten sliced with salt or in a peppery pork-bone soup.

places.name: Nambu Market sundae alley
places.note: Row of tiny market kitchens; cheap, fast and busiest around midday.

places.name: Nambu Market Night Market
places.note: Friday and Saturday night stalls with sundae, skewers and mandu alongside craft food.

places.name: Jungang-dong back lanes
places.note: Older downtown alleys with long-running sundae-guk shops open late.

food.name: Jeonju Choco Pie
food.desc: Not the supermarket snack: a bakery version with soft cocoa sponge, strawberry jam and thick cream, sold in boxes as the city's edible souvenir.

places.name: PNB Poongnyeon Jegwa
places.note: The original bakery that invented the Jeonju choco pie; expect a queue and boxes to go.

places.name: PNB Hanok Village branch
places.note: Convenient village outlet of the same bakery, also sells the famous baguette burger.

places.name: Gilgeori Yaja
places.note: Rival Jeonju choco pie maker with a fudgier, less sweet take worth comparing.

food.name: Hanok Village Street Food
food.desc: Grazing food along the village lanes: bibimbap croquettes, grilled cheese-and-galbi skewers, mandu, baguette burgers and hotteok.

places.name: Eunhaeng-ro food street
places.note: Main pedestrian run through the village, wall-to-wall snack stalls at weekends.

places.name: Nambu Market Cheongnyeon Mall
places.note: Young-traders' upstairs market with small kitchens and craft snacks, evenings mainly.

places.name: Jaman Mural Village lanes
places.note: Hillside cafes and snack shops just above the hanok village, quieter than the main street.

food.name: Makgeolli (Makgeolli Sang)
food.desc: Order a kettle of cloudy rice wine in Jeonju and a whole table of free anju arrives; each new kettle brings another round of dishes.

places.name: Samcheon-dong Makgeolli Alley
places.note: The classic makgeolli-sang street; go in a group, the food table is enormous.

places.name: Seosin-dong Makgeolli Alley
places.note: Second and slightly more central alley of makgeolli houses, busy from early evening.

places.name: Yetchon Makgeolli
places.note: Well-known house on the Samcheon alley, reliable for the full kettle-and-table ritual.

food.name: Moju
food.desc: Jeonju's warm spiced brew: leftover makgeolli simmered with ginger, cinnamon, jujube and liquorice until barely alcoholic, drunk with bean-sprout soup.

places.name: Waengi Kongnamul Gukbap
places.note: Traditional pairing, moju served warm in a small bowl with the morning soup.

places.name: Nambu Market stalls
places.note: Market vendors sell moju by the cup and in bottles to take home.

places.name: Hanok Village teahouses
places.note: Several village shops serve moju alongside traditional teas and rice cakes.

landmarks: Jeonju Hanok Village
Over 700 traditional tiled-roof houses form Korea's most atmospheric hanok quarter, best wandered in rented hanbok between teahouses and craft shops.
Gyeonggijeon Shrine
A tranquil 15th-century shrine complex of courtyards and bamboo groves enshrining the portrait of King Taejo, founder of the Joseon dynasty.
Jeondong Catholic Cathedral
A graceful Romanesque-Byzantine brick cathedral from 1914, built on martyrdom ground and beloved as one of Korea's most beautiful churches.
Omokdae and Imokdae Pavilions
Hilltop pavilions where dynasty founder Yi Seong-gye celebrated victory, now prized for sweeping sunset views over the hanok rooftops.
Pungnammun Gate
The last surviving gate of Jeonju's old city walls, a stately Joseon-era landmark glowing under floodlights each evening.
Jaman Mural Village
A hillside neighborhood transformed by whimsical murals and quirky cafés, tumbling down the slope just across from the hanok village.
Nambu Traditional Market
A century-old market famed for its Friday-and-Saturday night food alley, where young vendors reinvent Korean street eats.
Jeonju Hyanggyo
A serene Joseon-era Confucian school whose 400-year-old ginkgo trees blaze gold each autumn, a favorite drama filming location.
Deokjin Park
A romantic city park whose vast pond disappears beneath pink and white lotus blossoms every July, crossed by a suspension footbridge.
Wansan Park
A city-centre hill famed for its riotous spring display of double-flowering cherry blossoms layered over azalea slopes.

train.note: Jeonju station is about 3 km northeast of the Hanok Village, 10-15 minutes by city bus or taxi. Trains run down the Jeolla Line from Seoul's Yongsan station in roughly two hours on the fastest services, though some journeys involve a change at Iksan onto the Honam high-speed line. Reservations open about a month ahead and holiday weekends fill quickly, so book online rather than at the counter; the Korail Pass is valid on all these services. South Korea has no cross-border passenger trains.

bus.note: The Express Bus Terminal and the Intercity Bus Terminal stand side by side in Geumam-dong, about 2 km from the Hanok Village. Coaches from Seoul's Central City/Gangnam terminal start around 15,000 won and take 2.5 hrs, Busan takes about 3 hrs 20 min, and limousine buses from Incheon Airport leave every half hour for a 3.5-hour run. Express services are booked at Kobus (https://www.kobus.co.kr/) and intercity ones at Bustago (https://www.bustago.or.kr/). There are no international coach services from South Korea.

ferry.note: Jeonju is an inland provincial capital with no port. The closest sailings are from Gunsan, about an hour west, where the international terminal has a service to Shidao in China and local boats serve the Gogunsan islands, and from Mokpo further south for the Jeolla island network.

half.name: Maisan Provincial Park
half.blurb: Twin horse-ear-shaped peaks in Jinan County with the stacked stone pagodas of Tapsa temple at their base, about an hour from Jeonju.

half.name: Naejangsan National Park
half.blurb: A mountain park known for autumn foliage, temple trails, and a cable car, less than two hours south of Jeonju.

half.name: Sunchang
half.blurb: Korea's famous gochujang-making region, known for fermented red-pepper-paste villages and hands-on tasting workshops, about an hour from Jeonju.
